dmm-2021-team-01.title: Recurrence
dmm-2021-team-01.body:
Let $a_n$ be the number of ordered sequences of $1$s, $2$s and $3$s with sum $n$. Looking at the last score, $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+a_{n-3}$, with $a_0=1$ (so $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_3=4$). Then $a_4=7$, $a_5=13$, $a_6=24$, $a_7=44$, $a_8=81$.

**Answer: 81**

dmm-2021-team-02.title: Count coprime integers
dmm-2021-team-02.body:
$2021=43\cdot47$. The number of integers in $[1,2022]$ coprime to $2021$ is $2022-\lfloor\frac{2022}{43}\rfloor-\lfloor\frac{2022}{47}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{2022}{2021}\rfloor=2022-47-43+1=1933$, and $2022$ itself is coprime to $2021$, so it is the $1933$rd number in the list.

The first $n$ groups contain $1+3+\dots+(2n-1)=n^2$ numbers. Since $43^2=1849<1933\le1936=44^2$, the $1933$rd number is in group $k=44$.

**Answer: 44**

dmm-2021-team-03.title: Union of two circle segments
dmm-2021-team-03.body:
For $X$ above line $AB$, $\angle AXB\ge60^\circ$ exactly when $X$ lies inside the circle through $A,B$ whose major arc above $AB$ subtends $60^\circ$. By the extended sine rule its radius is $\rho=\frac{AB}{2\sin60^\circ}=\sqrt3$, its center is at distance $\sqrt{\rho^2-(3/2)^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ from $AB$ on the same side, and the chord $AB$ cuts off a minor segment of central angle $120^\circ$ on the other side.

The part of the region above $AB$ is therefore the disc minus that minor segment:
$$\pi\rho^2-\frac{\rho^2}{2}\left(\frac{2\pi}3-\sin120^\circ\right)=3\pi-\frac32\left(\frac{2\pi}3-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=2\pi+\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}.$$
By symmetry the part below $AB$ has the same area, so $[R]=4\pi+\frac{3\sqrt3}2\approx12.57+2.60=15.16$, and the closest integer is $15$.

**Answer: 15**

dmm-2021-team-04.title: Set up an equation
dmm-2021-team-04.body:
Let the number be $10^nd+k$ where $d$ is the leading digit and $k<10^n$ is the number left after erasing it. We need $10^nd+k=29k$, i.e. $28k=10^nd$, so $7k=\frac{10^nd}{4}$. Since $7\mid10^nd$ with $d\le9$, we need $7\mid d$, so $d=7$. Then $4k=10^n$, so $k=25\cdot10^{n-2}$ and $n\ge2$. The smallest choice $n=2$ gives $k=25$ and the number $725$ ($725=29\cdot25$).

**Answer: 725**

dmm-2021-team-05.title: Reflect the world
dmm-2021-team-05.body:
Instead of reflecting the light ray, keep it straight (the line $x=1$) and reflect the mirrors. Repeatedly reflecting the pair of mirrors across the mirror hit produces lines through the origin at angles $15^\circ,30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ,\dots$ (alternately images of the line $y=\tan15^\circ x$ and of the $x$-axis). The vertical ray crosses the $15^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ lines (these are the three reflections) and then hits the $60^\circ$ line, an image of the $x$-axis, so the screen is on the $x$-axis mirror. The hit point on the $60^\circ$ line is $(1,\sqrt3)$, at distance $2$ from the origin; in the real picture the screen is at distance $2$ from the origin on the $x$-axis: $(a,b)=(2,0)$.

So $10a^2+5b^2=40$.

**Answer: 40**

dmm-2021-team-05.title: Follow the ray directly
dmm-2021-team-05.body:
The ray from $(1,0)$ going up hits $y=\tan15^\circ x$ at $(1,0.268)$, then (after reflection) the $x$-axis at $(1.155,0)$, then the line again at $(1.366,0.366)$, and then the $x$-axis at $(2,0)$. That is $3$ reflections followed by the screen at $(2,0)$, so $10\cdot4+5\cdot0=40$.

**Answer: 40**

dmm-2021-team-06.title: Construction and a partition bound
dmm-2021-team-06.body:
Label unit cubes by coordinates $(x,y,z)\in\{1,\dots,5\}^3$. A cube is on the surface if some coordinate is $1$ or $5$.

**Construction.** Choose all cubes with all three coordinates in $\{1,3,5\}$ except the interior one $(3,3,3)$: $27-1=26$ cubes. Two of them differ by at least $2$ in some coordinate, so they share no vertex.

**Upper bound.** Partition the $98$ surface cubes into $26$ groups in which any two cubes share a vertex (so each group contains at most one chosen cube):

* $8$ corner groups: the $7$ surface cubes of each $2\times2\times2$ corner block;
* $12$ edge groups: for each edge, its middle cube together with its two neighbours (one on each of the two faces meeting at that edge) lying next to the middle cube;
* $6$ face groups: the central cube of each face.

Check: $8\cdot7+12\cdot3+6\cdot1=98$, and within each group any two cubes lie in a common $2\times2\times2$ block, so they share a vertex. Hence $m\le26$.

**Answer: 26**

dmm-2021-team-07.title: Telescoping
dmm-2021-team-07.body:
$\tan(2a_k)=\dfrac{2k}{1-k^2}=-\left(\dfrac1{k-1}+\dfrac1{k+1}\right)$. The sign $(-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1}$ is $-,-,+,+,-,-,\dots$ for $k=4,5,6,7,8,9,\dots$ (it is $-1$ for $k\equiv0,1$ and $+1$ for $k\equiv2,3\pmod4$). So the terms are
$$+\left(\tfrac13+\tfrac15\right)+\left(\tfrac14+\tfrac16\right)-\left(\tfrac15+\tfrac17\right)-\left(\tfrac16+\tfrac18\right)+\left(\tfrac17+\tfrac19\right)+\dots$$
The terms with odd denominators telescope to $\frac13$ and those with even denominators to $\frac14$ (the partial sums converge as the leftover terms tend to $0$). The sum is $\frac13+\frac14=\frac7{12}$, so $a+b=19$.

**Answer: 19**

dmm-2021-team-08.title: Residues modulo x
dmm-2021-team-08.body:
Note $101050=2021\cdot50$, so the $n$th debt is $2021\cdot50+n$, payable iff $2021\cdot50+n=2021a+xb$ with $a,b\ge0$ integers; then necessarily $a\le50$, i.e. $n\equiv-2021\,j\pmod x$ for some $j=50-a\in\{0,\dots,50\}$ (and conversely such $j$ gives $b\ge0$).

* If $43\mid x$ or $47\mid x$: every payable amount is a multiple of $43$ (resp. $47$), but $101051\equiv1\pmod{43}$ and $\pmod{47}$ (since $2021$ is a multiple of both), so person $1$ cannot be paid.
* If $\gcd(x,2021)=1$ and $x\le51$: $2021$ is invertible mod $x$, so $2021j$ for $j=0,\dots,x-1$ hits every residue and everybody can be paid.
* If $\gcd(x,2021)=1$ and $x\ge52$: $2021j$ takes at most $51$ residues mod $x$, but $n=1,\dots,52$ are $52$ different residues, so someone cannot be paid.

So the bad values are the multiples of $43$ or $47$ and all $x\ge52$; the four smallest are $43,47,52,53$, with sum $195$.

**Answer: 195**

dmm-2021-team-08.title: Brute force
dmm-2021-team-08.body:
Checking every $x$ and every $n=1,\dots,90$ by computer (is $101050+n$ of the form $2021a+xb$?) shows that the smallest $x$ with an unpayable debt are $43,47,52,53$, so the sum is $195$.

**Answer: 195**

dmm-2021-team-09.title: Every path has the same probability
dmm-2021-team-09.body:
To stop at $(k,10)$ the frog goes from $(1,1)$ to $(k,9)$ and then steps up. The path has $k-1$ right-steps and $9$ up-steps in total. Along a path, the denominators $x+y$ are $2,3,\dots,k+9$ (product $(k+9)!$), and the numerators are $1,2,\dots,k-1$ for the right steps and $1,2,\dots,9$ for the up steps. So every such path has probability $\dfrac{(k-1)!\,9!}{(k+9)!}$. The number of paths to $(k,9)$ is $\binom{k+7}{8}$, hence
$$P(\text{stop at }x=k)=\binom{k+7}8\frac{(k-1)!\,9!}{(k+9)!}=\frac{9}{(k+8)(k+9)}=9\left(\frac1{k+8}-\frac1{k+9}\right).$$
Summing for $k=1,\dots,15$ telescopes: $9\left(\frac19-\frac1{24}\right)=1-\frac38=\frac58$. So $m+n=13$.

**Answer: 13**

dmm-2021-team-09.title: Exact dynamic programming
dmm-2021-team-09.body:
Define $f(x,y)$ as the probability of finishing with $x<16$ from $(x,y)$. Computing this recursion exactly with fractions from $(1,1)$ gives $\frac58$, in agreement, so $m+n=13$.

**Answer: 13**

dmm-2021-team-10.title: Homothety
dmm-2021-team-10.body:
Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and let $D$ be the second intersection of line $ZX$ with $\omega$. The circle $XYZ$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $Z$, so the homothety centred at $Z$ taking the circle $XYZ$ to $\omega$ sends $X\mapsto D$ and $Y\mapsto A$ (as $Y$ lies on line $ZA$). Therefore $XY\parallel DA$, i.e. $AD\parallel BC$.

Since also $DX\parallel AC$ (because $XZ\parallel AC$), $ACXD$ is a parallelogram: $DX=AC=455$ and $AD=CX$.

The chords $AD$ and $BC$ of $\omega$ are parallel, so reflection in the common perpendicular bisector swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$ and $A\leftrightarrow D$. By the cosine rule $\cos B=\frac{585^2+520^2-455^2}{2\cdot585\cdot520}=\frac23$, so the foot of $A$ on $BC$ is at distance $585\cdot\frac23=390$ from $B$; the foot of $D$ is its mirror image, at distance $520-390=130$ from $B$. Hence $AD=390-130=260=CX$, so $X$ is the midpoint of $BC$ with $XB=XC=260$.

Power of the point $X$ with respect to $\omega$: $XZ\cdot XD=XB\cdot XC=260^2$, so $XZ=\frac{67600}{455}=\frac{1040}7$ and $ZD=ZX+XD=\frac{1040}7+455$. From the homothety, $\dfrac{XY}{DA}=\dfrac{ZX}{ZD}$, so
$$XY=260\cdot\frac{1040/7}{1040/7+455}=\frac{260\cdot1040}{1040+3185}=64.$$

**Answer: 64**

dmm-2021-team-10.title: Numerical check
dmm-2021-team-10.body:
Placing $B=(0,0)$, $C=(520,0)$ and $A$ from the side lengths, one can search for the point $Y$ on $BC$ for which the circle through $X,Y,Z$ (with $X$ on $BC$ and $XZ\parallel AC$) is tangent to the circumcircle at $Z$. The condition holds for $X=(260,0)$ and $Y=(324,0)$, giving $XY=64$.

**Answer: 64**
